title: Engineering Bimetallic Copper-Tin Based Core-Shell Alloy@Oxide Nanowire as Efficient Catalyst for Electrochemical CO2 Reduction
abstract: Pursuing both high effective and selective electrocatalysts is significant for efficient and low-cost electrochemical carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction. Here, we design a novel bimetallic alloy/oxide nanowire catalyst with core-shell configuration. A typical CuSn alloy core provides high electrical conductivity while the amorphous Cu doped SnO2 shell guarantees the catalytic activity and selectivity for CO2 reduction process. Computational studies further elucidate the important role of Cu doped SnO2 layer in the electrocatalytic selectivity for formate and the restraint of hydrogen production. Benefited from the well-designed components and hierarchical configuration, the as-prepared electrocatalyst displays a partial current density of 30 mAcm 2 with a Faradaic efficiency of 78% at 0.9 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) for formate. This work provides a new pathway to design advanced electrocatalyst for CO2 electrochemical reduction.

sections.heading: Engineering Bimetallic Copper-Tin Based Core-Shell Alloy@Oxide Nanowire as Efficient Catalyst for Electrochemical CO2 Reduction
sections.text:

Pursuing both high effective and selective electrocatalysts is significant for efficient and low-cost electrochemical carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction. sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
As a greenhouse gas, carbon dioxide (CO2) has caused a series of environmental problems such as global warming, rainwater acidification, sea-level rise and so forth.[1] In 2020, the CO2 content in the atmosphere has reached 415 ppm with far exceeding of safety limit, and still increased.[2] Therefore, it is imperative to reduce CO2 level in the atmosphere. A promising strategy is the conversion of CO2 into high valuable fuels and chemicals. Until now, various CO2 conversion methods have been widely investigated such as thermochemical, photochemical, electrochemical approaches, etc.[3] Among them, electrochemical CO2 conversion has aroused considerable attention owing to its achievable conversion efficiencies under ambient conditions. More importantly, the reaction rate and product categories of electrochemical CO2 conversion can be facilely controlled by enough external bias on the reaction chambers with appropriate catalysts.[4] So far, many metal-based electrodes have been used as catalysts for electrochemical reduction of CO2 (CO2RR). For example, some noble metals (i. e., Au,[5] Ag[6] and Pd[7]) are favorable for the reduction of CO2 to CO while the main group metals (i. e., Sn,[8] Pb,[9] In[10] and Bi[11]) can be used for catalyzing CO2 reduction to form formate. In particular, Cu-based catalysts have aroused special attention for the CO2RR due to the various potential products, including carbon monoxide, formate, methane, ethylene, and other hydrocarbons.[12] Among these products, formate is an important chemical and widely used in the field of pharmaceuticals, textile industries, fuel cell and so forth.[13] In order to achieve high value-added formate, the product selectivity of Cu-based catalyst needs further optimization. Besides, some other drawbacks such as high overpotential and unavoidable side reaction (i. e., hydrogen evolution reaction, HER) also severely block the development of Cu-based catalysts. Hence, it is significant to design novel Cu-based electrocatalysts for high-efficiency CO2RR with high formate selectivity.
Nowadays, it has been recognized that elemental doping can effectively modulate the electronic and geometric factors of materials to improve the electrocatalytic performance of Cubased catalysts. In general, Sn-based electrodes possess a high selectivity for formate generation during the CO2RR process, [14] however, the depicted low activity is undesirable.[15] Therefore, designing Cu Sn based composites would be a prospective pathway to construct high-performance CO2RR catalysts with both good electrocatalytic activity and selectivity.[16] Benefiting from the synergistic effect of different metallic components, Cu Sn based electrocatalysts can weaken the binding strength of both CO and adsorbed hydrogen (H*).[17] Therefore, it not only effectively suppresses the side HER but also improves the catalytic activity and formate selectivity for CO2RR. ductivity and low active site of Sn-oxides results in unsatisfied performance of CO2RR. Many strategies have been devoted to modifying the conductivity and electrocatalytic activity of oxides layer, including heteroatoms/vacancies insertion and nano-structure construction.[13b,18] For example, Hu et al.[19]
introduced Cu and S atoms into the SnO2 catalyst, thereby achieving efficient performance for the reduction of CO2 to formate at low overpotential. Li and co-workers[20] revealed that the thinner Cu doped SnO2 shell (0.8 nm) could lead to the preferential CO production whereas thicker SnO2 shell (1.8 nm) preferred to form formate. In addition, Kumar[21] reported a novel reduced SnO2 nanowires catalyst with a high density of grain boundaries which showed a high Faradaic efficiency for the formation of HCOOH. Based on these discussions, the combination of surface modification and structure engineering to optimize the catalytic performance of Cu Sn based materials is highly promising but remains a huge challenge to date.
Herein, a kind of novel Cu Sn alloy nanowires coated by Cu-doped amorphous oxide (Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2) skin was constructed as efficient CO2RR electrocatalyst. The inner alloy core with high electronic conductivity can promote the rapid electron transfer to the Cu doped SnO2 layer. Meanwhile, the Cu doped SnO2 superficial layer with large electrochemical active surface area significantly enhances the electrocatalytic activity for CO2 reduction process. With the above advantages, the as-prepared Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 electrode achieves a high partial current density of 30 mAcm 2 for yielding formate with a great Faradaic efficiency of 78.6% at 0.90 V (vs. RHE). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that the Cu doped SnO2 domain not only depicted lower Gibbs free energy of HCOOH but also enhanced the intermediate product for CO formation, thereby improving the activity and selectivity of formate.

sections.heading: 2. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
As schematically illustrated in Figure 1, the Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 catalyst was fabricated by a facile hydrothermal method using Cu nanowire as template. Firstly, copper nanowires (Cu NWs) array was in-situ formed on the Cu foam (CF). After that, the surrounding Cu NWs was transformed into Cu3Sn alloy via a hydrothermal method in virtue of the neighbouring Sn source. Noted that the amorphous SnO2 shell was concomitantly developed on the Cu3Sn alloy surface because the Sn atom was prone to aggregating and oxidizing on the outer layer for low
surface energy.[22] For the inner Cu3Sn core, the subsequent diffusion of Sn atoms from the inner to the outer layer as well as the residual Cu atoms both contributes to the formation of amorphous Cu doped SnO2 shell. Therefore, a unique coreshell-type Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs hierarchical structure was obtained.
The crystal structures of the as-obtained samples were firstly investigated by the X-ray diffraction (XRD) (Figure S1). As shown in the XRD patterns, the Cu(OH)2 NWs was successfully synthesized coupled with the following evolved Cu NWs as well (Figure S1a). For the XRD patterns of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 and Cu3Sn/CF (Figure S1b), the main diffraction peaks of Cu3Sn@CuSnO2 located at 43.4°, 50.6° and 74.4°, being assigned to the (111), (200) and (220) planes of metallic CF network (PDF#042090).[23] The other additional peaks at 37.93°, 41.78°, 43.44°, 57.63°, 68.46° and 77.44° can be identified as the (020), (002), (211), (212), (230) and (213) plane of Cu3Sn (PDF# 04-2885). Owing to the amorphous characteristic of Cu doped SnO2 shell, the diffraction peaks referring to SnO2 were hard to be recognized. The same diffraction peaks were also observed on the Cu3Sn/CF reference sample, verifying the same formation of Cu3Sn phase and amorphous Cu SnO2.
The surface morphologies of all samples were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Before the treatment, a smooth skeleton surface of Cu foam was observed (Figure S2a and b). Figure 2a displays uniform and high-density Cu(OH)2 NWs grown on the skeleton surface of Cu foam. After the thermal reduction in H2/Ar atmosphere, the Cu(OH)2 NWs were reduced to Cu NWs with well retention of nanowires topography (Figure 2b). After the introduction of Sn in the hydrothermal reaction, core-shell-type Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs were generated, together with that the nanowires became a bit coarse and bent to form network structure (Figure 2c). As a comparison, the developed Cu3Sn/CF exhibits no nanowire structure but a coarser skeleton surface was obtained (Figure S2c and d). It is obvious the as-fabricated core-shell-type Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs catalyst can not only provide abundant catalytic active-sites but also facilitate the mass supply and transfer. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image also

discloses the typical core-shell structure of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs catalyst with the mean diameter of ca. 130 nm (Figure 2d). High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image (Figure 2e) further reveals that the Cu3Sn alloy core was coated by amorphous Cu SnO2 shell with a thickness of ca. 6 nm. The lattice fringe spacing with about 0.216 nm in the inner crystalline core was assigned to the (002) facet of Cu3Sn. The selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 also demonstrate the existence of metallic Cu and Cu3Sn phase (Figure 2f), which is consistent with XRD measurements. The STEM-energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) elemental mapping of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 (Figure 2g) displays the Cu, Sn and O elements were uniformly distributed throughout the nanowires. Moreover, the typical core-shell structure of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 was also verified by the EDX linear scan profile (Figure S3a and b), in which major O elements with partial Cu and Sn elements are observed around the nanowires. The elemental linear result further manifests the successful construction of superficial Cu SnO2 active layer. Meanwhile, EDX spectrum exhibits that the average atomic ratio of Cu: Sn: O was determined to 57: 22: 20, revealing the coexistence of Cu3Sn and SnO2 phases (Figure S3c). This was further elucidated based upon the XPS measurements.
The chemical states of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs were further measured by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The survey spectrum in Figure 3a evidences the presence of Cu, Sn and O elements in Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs. As shown in Figure 3b, the XPS spectrum of Sn 3d can be fitted into two peaks at 494.56 eV and 486.15 eV, being assigned to the 3d3/2 and 3d5/2 peaks of Sn4+, while the shoulder peaks at 492.77 eV and 484.33 eV are related to metallic Sn0.[24] In the O 1s spectrum (Figure 3c), three distinct peaks at 529.83, 531.26 and 533.09 eV derive from O Sn4+, adsorbed oxygen and oxygen vacancies in the Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs, respectively.
[14a,25] These results still confirm the existence of SnO2 on the Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 catalyst. For the Cu 2p spectrum (Figure 3d), the two peaks located at 952.13 eV and 932.31 eV, corresponding to Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/ 2 of Cu
0,[26] while the other two peaks located at 953.55 eV and 933.80 eV were represented for Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2 of Cu 2+.
The zero-valent Sn0 and Cu0 originate from the Cu Sn alloys core while trace Cu2+ was from the outer oxides layer due to the copper atoms diffusion and oxidization. The XPS spectra also indicate that the Cu3Sn/CF sample without NWs topography also possessed a similar distribution of valence states with Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs (Figure S4a and b), conforming to the XRD analysis.
The electrochemical activities of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs and Cu3Sn/CF towards the CO2RR were firstly evaluated by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV, Figure 4a). The reduction current in Ar-saturated solution was ascribed to the single HER. It is obvious that the reduction current increased dramatically in the CO2-saturated solution compared to that in Ar-saturated solution, demonstrating the CO2RR occurred preferentially over HER on the catalysts. Moreover, in the CO2-saturated solution, the Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs catalyst displayed higher reduction current than that of Cu3Sn/CF, indicating the superior catalytic activity of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs catalyst toward CO2RR.
Furthermore, chronoamperometry (i–t) were used to identify and quantify the CO2RR products on Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 catalyst biased at a series of selected potentials between 0.5 and 1.0 V (Figure S5). It is clear that all of curves manifest good stability for at least 2 hours. Based upon the products analysis, it is found that the major CO2RR products on Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs catalyst was HCOO , CO and H2, and their total measured overall FEs was located at the range of 90–100%. As exhibited in Figure 4b and c, the Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs endowed with

of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs (~30 mAcm
2) is much higher than that of Cu3Sn/CF (~10 mAcm
2) at 0.9 V (Figure 3d), further testifying the enhanced catalytic activity and selectivity of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NW toward the CO2RR. Moreover, the catalytic performance of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 is superior or comparable to that of previously reported catalysts, including Cu3Sn alloy (FEHCOO =50%, jHCOO =1.4 mAcm 2),[27] Cu6Sn5 NPs/CB (FEHCOO =65.3%, jHCOO
=7.5 mAcm 2),[28] CuSn NPs/C A (FEHCOO =71.5%, jHCOO =12.6 mAcm 2)[29] and so forth (Figure 4e and Table S1). The good catalytic activity should derive from the typical core-shell nanowire structure and Cu doped SnO2 amorphous layer, which is beneficial to both depress the HER process and promote the conversion from CO2 to formate.
Furthermore, double layer capacitance (Cdl) is generally utilized to reflect the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) of catalysts.[30] As depicted in Figure S6, the Cdl of Cu3Sn@CuSnO2 was determined to 29.73 mFcm
2, being greater than that of the Cu3Sn/CF (1.77 mFcm
2) and Cu NWs (21.39 mFcm 2). The high ECSA of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 catalyst should benefit from the unique core-shell nanowire structure. On the one hand, it can provide abundant active sites for CO2RR and guarantee the sufficient contact between catalyst and electrolyte. On the other hand, the network structure with quantities of nanowires can greatly restrict the diffusion of OH , leading to the increase of local pH and thus suppressing side HER.[31] Meanwhile, the coreshell-type Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs can accelerate the formation of intermediate and enhance the reaction kinetic of CO2RR. The charge transfer behavior of as-obtained catalysts for CO2RR was investigated by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analysis. Nyquist plots obtained at 0.9 V for all samples were represented in Figure S7. The Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs exhibits the lowest interface charge-transfer resistance (Rct), implying the faster electron transfer during the CO2RR process. This should be originated from the fast electron transport along the onedimensional path and the tight contact between Cu3Sn core and SnO2 shell.
[32] In this case, the smart structure engineering can not only suppress HER to accelerate CO2RR, but also increase the intrinsic activity and reaction kinetic for CO2RR process.
In order to evaluate the stability of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs catalyst, a long-term electrolysis was performed at a constant potential of 0.9 V for CO2RR. In this process, the electrolyte refreshing, and product analysis were conducted every 2 hours. The oscillation of current density at high potentials derives from both the rapid rotation of electrolyte and gas bubbles blocking of part active sites. As exhibited in Figure 4f, the Faradaic efficiency for formate generation remained above 70% without obvious oscillations during the electrolysis operation for 12 hours, indicating the excellent durability of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs catalyst. Meanwhile, the typical nanowires topography was preserved well even after the long-time electrolysis operation
(Inset in Figure 4f). Thus, it further verifies the good physicochemical stability of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs catalyst for CO2RR.
As a comparison, the competitive HER was the dominating reduction process on pure Cu NWs, verifying the key role of amorphous oxide layer in Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 for CO2RR process (Figure S8). In order to further explore the important function of Cu SnO2 oxide layer in CO2RR process, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out to investigate the effect of Cu doping on the Gibbs free energy of intermediates for CO2RR. The slab models were constructed on (110) plane of Cu doped SnO2 and pure SnO2. Herein, two Sn atoms were replaced by two Cu atoms on the SnO2 (110) plane to signify the Cu doping.
The Gibbs free energy diagrams and the corresponding adsorption configurations of CO2RR process on pure SnO2 and different site of Cu doped SnO2 are shown in Figure 5, Figure S9, S10 and S11, respectively. For both Cu doped SnO2 Sn site and pure SnO2, the formation of intermediate HCOO* is an exothermic process while the Cu doped SnO2 Cu site is endothermic and HCOO* hydrogenation is the potential determining step (PDS) for the formate path. For another, both of the formation of COOH* and H* are endothermic processes. Meanwhile, COOH* and H* generation are the PDS for producing CO and H2 respectively. Furthermore, the Cu site and Sn site of Cu doped SnO2 show superior inhibition of hydrogen evolution over oxide surface. Compared with SnO2, both Cu site and Sn site of Cu doped SnO2 weakens the energy barrier of HCOOH formation and increases the binding energies of intermediates COOH* and H*. Also, Cu site in Sn oxide exhibits lower energy barrier of HCOO* formation and higher energy barrier of COOH* formation than Sn site. These beneficial factors contribute to the decrease of limiting potential for HCOOH generation, as well as the superior inhibition for the formation of CO and H2, thus enhancing the Faraday efficiency of formate.

sections.heading: 3. Conclusions
sections.text: In summary, a novel bimetallic core-shell-type Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 nanowire electrode was constructed as efficient catalyst for CO2RR with high formate selectivity. Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 NWs exhibit a current density of 30 mAcm 2 and Faraday efficiency of 78% at 0.9 V (vs. RHE). The promising CO2RR performance should be attributed to the following advantages: (a) the selfstanding electrode provides fast pathway for electron transport and mass diffusion; (b) high-density nanowire array not only ensures the efficient contact between abundant catalytic sites and reactant for CO2RR reaction, but also restrains the side HER process; (c) the well-designed core-shell structure offers the Cu3Sn alloy core with high conductivity and amorphous Sn oxides shell with high catalytic activity; (d) the Cu dopant embedded in the oxide shell facilitates the catalytic selectivity by both promoting HCOO* to formate and inhibiting the COOH* dissociation for CO production, as well as suppresses the formation of H2. This work provides a novel thought for the design of advanced electrocatalysts for CO2 electrochemical reduction.

sections.heading: Chemicals and Materials
sections.text: Stannous chloride dihydrate (SnCl2 · 2H2O), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3), ammonium persulphate ((NH4)2S2O8), sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and potassium hydroxide (KOH) were obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Cu foam (CF) with a thickness of 1.5 mm was bought from Yu Xing Co., Ltd. Argon (Ar, 99.99%), carbon dioxide (CO2, 99.99%) and H2/Ar mixture (5 vol% H2/Ar) were purchased from Anxu Hongyun Technology Co., Ltd. (Taiyuan, China). 115 Nafion membrane was obtained from Shanghai Hesen Electric Co., Ltd. All chemicals were analytical grade and used without further purification. Deionized water was supplied by an Ultrapure water system (18.25 MΩcm).

sections.heading: Fabrication of Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 and Cu3Sn/CF
sections.text:
Firstly, Cu foam (CF) was immersed into a mixed solution containing 0.133 M (NH4)2S2O8 and 2.667 M NaOH for 15 min. Then the priortreated Cu foam was successively rinsed with de-ionized (DI) water and absolute ethanol, and dried in nitrogen atmosphere. The CF turned to deep blue color, which indicates the formation of Cu(OH)2 nanowire arrays on the surface.[33] After that, Cu nanowires (NWs) were obtained by annealing the Cu(OH)2 NWs at 200 °C for 4 hours with a heating rate of 5 °Cmin 1 at H2/Ar atmosphere.
To fabricate core-shell-type Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2, the above as-prepared Cu NWs sample was further immersed into a 40 mL mixed solution (0.4 M SnCl2 +3 M KOH) and then kept at 180 °C for 12 hours in autoclave (50 mL) for hydrothermal treatment. After cooling to ambient temperature, the as-formed Cu3Sn@Cu-SnO2 sample was washed several times with ultrapure water and ethanol, and dried. As a comparison, Cu3Sn/CF was also prepared by the identical hydrothermal treatment on bare Cu foam substrate.

sections.heading: Characterization
sections.text: The phase of as-prepared catalysts was characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD, DX-2700 X-ray diffractometer) at 40 kV and 30 mA with Cu Kα radiation. Morphologies and chemical compositions were analyzed by a scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, ZEISS MERLIN Compact). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were attained by a FEI Talos S-FEG microscope operating with an accelerating voltage of 200 kV, equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) analyzer. Chemical states and compositions were analyzed by an X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (ThermoFischer, ESCALAB250Xi) with Al Kα radiation at 12.5 kV and 16 mA. The binding energy was calibrated by using the C 1s at 284.6 eV as the reference.

sections.heading: Electrochemical Measurement for CO2RR and Product Analysis
sections.text:
The electrochemical measurement was conducted by using a 30 mL two-compartment electrolysis cell, separated by a Nafion 115 membrane. The electrocatalytic CO2RR reaction was conducted in a CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution (pH=7.2) purged with continuous CO2 gas flow (20 mL min
1). During the reaction, the electrolyte was stirred at 900 rpm in the cathode chamber to which a gas chromatograph was connected. The as-prepared self-supported catalyst was used as the working electrode with a geometric surface area of 1 cm2. A saturated Ag/AgCl electrode and platinum plate were applied as the reference and counter electrodes, respectively. All the potentials were controlled by an electrochemical workstation (CorrTest, Wuhan). The measured electrode potentials were converted to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) through the following formula:
ERHE ¼ EAg=AgCl þ 0:197þ 0:0591� pH (1)
The performance of electrochemical CO2RR was tested via potentiostatic polarization at various working potentials (i. e., 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9 V vs. RHE) for 2 hours. All the catalysts were first electrochemically activated via cyclic voltammetry cycling until stable profiles were obtained. Then, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was carried out in a potential range from 0 to 1.0 V at a scan rate of 30 mVs 1 in Ar- or CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution. Double layer capacitance (Cdl) was determined by cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurement at various scan rates (20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 mVs 1) in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed within a frequency range of 0.01 Hz–200 MHz in a CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution. All the gas and liquid products were collected and analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) and 1H liquid nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR).
Gas chromatograph (GC-7820, Zhongkehuifen, China) equipped with both thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and flame ionization detector (FID) was used to quantify the gas-phase products. The FEi of gas product species-CO and H2 was calculated by [34]
FEi ¼ ðni � F� P� v � ciÞ=ðR� T � jÞ � 100 % (2)
Where ni is the number of electrons required to form one mole of the product and equal to 2 for both H2 and CO, F is the Faraday constant (96485.3 C mol 1), v is the volumetric flow rate of effluent gas measured using a mass flowmeter, ci is measured concentration of the gas product species by the GC, R is the ideal gas constant (8.314 Jmol 1 K 1). P and T are the ambient pressure (1 atm) and temperature (22 °C), respectively. j is the total current intensity.

Liquid products were characterized by 1H NMR on Bruker DRX 400 Advance. Liquid samples were treated for the NMR analysis by adding 2.5 mL of the catholyte in 500 μL of heavy water (D2O, 99.9 atom% D, Sigma-Aldrich) mixed with 0.05 vol% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 99.99%, Sigma-Aldrich). The amounts of formate were calculated by comparing the integral areas of observed formate peak with DMSO peak. The peak position for formate was calibrated using formic acid (HCOOH, 98%, Sigma-Aldrich) dissolved in 0.5 M KHCO3 solution containing the internal standard solution outlined above. The FEHCOO of formate was calculated by:
FEHCOO ¼ ðnHCOO � cHCOO � F� VcatholyteÞ=Qtotal � 100 % (3)
where nHCOO is 2, cHCOO is the concentration of formate in the catholyte determined by NMR, Vcatholyte is the total volume of catholyte in the H-type cell (25 mL), and Qtotal is the total charge passed during the CO2RR measurement.

sections.heading: Computational Details
sections.text:
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the Vienna Ab initial simulation package (VASP) code, which adopted the plane-wave basis set and the pseudopotential of the projector augmented wave (PAW) method.[35] The exchangecorrelation functionals were the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) and Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE).[36] The dispersion correction was considered through zero damping DFT-D3 method. The plane-wave kinetic cut-off energy was set at 400 eV with σ value of 0.02 eV in all systems. A (2×2×1) gamma centered k-mesh samplings were used for the SnO2 (110) and Cu doped SnO2 (110) slab. The surface of SnO2 (110) was modeled by five-atom layer model with the top three layers relaxed and the other layers fixed. All structures were relaxed until the convergence threshold reached to10 5 eV in energy and 0.02 eV/Å in force. The raw calculation data (E) of Eslab, EHCOO*, EH*, ECOOH* and ECO* is presented in Table S2.
In this work, the free energy diagrams for CO2 reduction use socalled “Computational Hydrogen Electrode” (CHE) model based on the following reaction:
Hþ þ e $ H2 ðgÞ=2 (4)
The CO2RR for generating formate and CO were assumed to be:
CO2 ðgÞ þ 2ðH þ þ e Þ þ * ! HCOO* þ ðHþ þ e Þ ! * þ HCOOH ðaqÞ (5)
CO2 ðgÞ þ 2ðHþ þ e Þ þ * ! COOH* þ ðHþ þ e Þ ! CO* þ H2O! * þ CO ðgÞ (6)
where * represents the surface adsorption site.[20]
The Gibbs free energy was calculated based on the formula below:
G ¼ EDFT þ EZPE TSþ CpdT (7)
where EDFT, EZPE, S and Cp were the electronic energy, zero-point energy, entropy and heat capacity, respectively. For adsorption intermediates, EZPE, S and Cp were determined by the vibration frequency calculation of the standard method. EZPE, S and Cp were referred to the reports by Klinkova et al. and Wang et al., as shown in Table S3.[29,37] Additionally, the stabilization for CO* and HCOO* were 0.1 eV owing to solvation corrections, while that for COOH* was 0.25 eV.[38]
